A B S T R A C T
In this study, the effects of annealing temperature on microstructure and mechanical properties of Fe–9Mn–5Al-
0.3C (wt.%) low density steel plates via intercritical quenching-annealing process were investigated through
field-emission scanning electron microscopy, electron backscatter diffraction. X-ray diffraction, and tensile tests
The results showed that the experimental steel maintained micro-laminated microstructure after intercritical
quenching-annealing treatment, consisting of δ-ferrite band and tempered martensite lamellar. After annealing at
the range of 600–800 <sup>◦</sup>C following quenching of 1050 <sup>◦</sup>C, tempered martensite lamellar mainly changed, and
affected the mechanical properties of the steel. The annealed experimental steels exhibited wide vield strength
grades (460–620 MPa) with excellent ductility (40–63 %) and low yield-tensile ratio (0.65–0.75). The proportion
of austenite, the density of geometrically necessary dislocations, and high-angle grain boundary density of
tempered martensite region as well as the presence or absence of carbides, were considered to contributed to the
mechanical properties. Austenitic mechanical ability was analyzed. Various annealed temperature led to the
different levels of austenitic stability through changing the enrichment of alloyed elements in austenite, further
causing different degrees of TRIP effect. TWIP effect existed during deformation according to estimation of SFE.
The steel annealed at 740 <sup>◦</sup>C had maximum uniform elongation (62.4 %) and the highest product of strength and
elongation (45.2 GPa%), depending on the maximum proportion of austenite transformed into martensite during
deformation. However. the 680 °C annealed steel with the highest austenitic stability exhibited deficient TRIP
effect, leading to the occurrence of necking. Moreover, work hardening behavior and fracture morphology of the
experimental steel were analyzed.

sumption and carbon emission. Fe–Mn–Al–C steel was a promising type
of steel with low density due to Al addition and high strength [1,2]. A
1.3 % reduction in density of steel could be obtained per 1 wt% addition
of Al [3]. The Al addition promoted the form of δ-ferrite, but facilitated
the nucleation of short-range order structure, which was harmful for
ductility of metal. Therefore, Mn, as an austenite stabilization element,
was usually added to steel together with Al. According to the content of
Al and Mn, low density steel was classified into four categories: ferritic
steels [4,5], ferritic-based duplex steels [6,7], austenite-based duplex
steels [2,8], and austenite steels [9–11]. Given that low weldability and

Dual-phase low density steel composed of δ-ferrite and martensite/
austenite was usually rolled and formed micro-laminated structure
under deformation [16–19]. Below the homogenization temperature, it
was difficult to refine δ-ferrite through recrystallization or phase
transformation. Therefore, improving prior austenite area was an
important method to enhance mechanical properties. Retained austenite
could improve mechanical properties of steel by transformation induced
plasticity (TRIP) and twinning induced plasticity (TWIP) [20–23]. The
mechanical stability of retained austenite had been widely investigated
. Xu et al. [26] revealed the correlation between deformation
behavior and austenite stability in Mn–Al type TRIP steel. Inhomoge
neous stability of retained austenite could lead to inhomogeneous and
discontinuous work hardening behavior, while the heterogeneity of
austenitic grain size and the orientation of retained austenite played
important roles in determining the stability of austenite when defor
mation. Chen et al. [27] reported that duplex lightweight steel of
Fe–8Mn–6Al-0.4C exhibited excellent mechanical properties of tensile
strength ~756 MPa and ~56 % elongation under synergy of TRIP and
TWIP effects.
The different proportions of soft phase and hard phase in Micro-
laminated low-density steel could lead to different mechanical proper
ties. Shang et al. [28] changed the δ-ferrite content by various quenching
temperature and tempering treatment to improve the mechanical
properties of laminar low density steel. The total elongation of the steel
was boosted from 4 % of hot-rolled state to 40 % of quenched-tempered
state. Xu et al. [29] increased the retained austenitic content of
micro-laminated low density steel by direction quenching and inter
critical annealing, which improving the ductility form 13 %–41 % in
total elongation under the assistance of TRIP effect.
In this study, the heat-treatment experiments of intercritical
quenching (IQ) and annealing were carried out on the steel of
Fe–9Mn–5Al-0.3C. The tensile strength, 0.2 % off-set yield strength, and
total elongation of the experimental steel were investigated corre
sponding to the relevant laminated microstructure. The relationship
between laminated microstructure and mechanical properties and the
effects of the austenitic stability on deformation behavior were dis
cussed. The main purpose of this research was to obtain better me
chanical properties and heat-treatment parameters of the experimental
steel to broaden its practical application.

Annealing process following IQ process considerably improved the
comprehensive mechanical properties of the steel in this study, but
decreased the yield strength of QA specimens. On the one hand, during
annealing processing, retained austenite fraction after quenching
increased, while reverted austenite nucleated and grew up at martensite
lath gaps, with the diffusion of the carbon and manganese into austenite
grains, and aluminum into martensite and ferrite. It was widely accepted
that ductile deformation started in soft phase universally, such as ferrite,
austenite [45]. With increase of annealing temperature, the fraction of
austenite gradually increased until QA-800 (Table 2). That the soft phase
of austenite increasing will be prone to induce ductile deformation,
leading to yield strength decreasing. On the other hand, recovery effect
of annealing treatment led to the decrease of the GND density in
tempered martensite and austenite. With the increase of annealing
temperature, the martensitic and austenitic GND values of annealed
specimens decreased continuously. The decrease of the GND density will
be easier to cause dislocation slip during deformation, decreasing the
yield strength of tempered martensite lamellar. Low GND density in
tempered martensite promoted the coordinate deformation between
tempered martensite and δ-ferrite band, which was beneficial to plas
ticity of the steel [28].
Therefore, the fraction of austenite, and the GND density of tempered
martensite lamellar are the mainly reasons of decreasing yield strength
of the experimental steel by annealing process. Furthermore, for QA-
620, the precipitation of carbides strongly retarded dislocation gliding
to greatly enhance yield and tensile strength, while the decrease of alloy
elements content in matrix reduced the lattice distortion of tempered
martensite to rise the deformability of the steel, which was positive to
the ductility. For QA-800, though its austenite fraction was slightly
lower than that of QA-740, its GND densities of tempered martensite and
austenite was lower, still leading to lower YS.

yield strength grades (460–620 MPa) under the conditions of
extremely excellent ductility and low yield-to-tensile ratio, could
substituted for TRIP 580T/400Y high strength automobile plates.
Specifically, the

annealed specimens decreased as annealing temperature, which
attributed to the factors of the proportion of austenite, geomet
rically necessary dislocations density, and block boundary den
sity of tempered martensite.
(3) The partitioning of C and Mn elements significantly affected the
mechanical stability of austenite. Specifically, austenite in the
specimen annealed at 680 <sup>◦</sup>C possessed the highest stability. With
annealing temperature increasing from
6 8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,

ity decreased due to the dilution of austenitic alloy elements.
When annealed at
6 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,
precipitated carbides in specimens led
to the decrease of alloy elements in matrix, resulting in lower
austenitic stability than that of 680 <sup>◦</sup>C annealed specimens.
Various austenitic stability contributed to various levels of TRIP
effect during deformation.
(4) All annealed specimens exhibited three-stage work hardening
characteristics, in which stage II and III resulted from the
competition between dislocation gliding and TRIP effect, com
bined with the assistance of TWIP effect according to SFEs. The
specimen annealed only at 680 <sup>◦</sup>C exhibited apparently necking
due to deficient TRIP effect, and afterward underwent a second
stage of uniform elongation until failure.
